clinicalPearls: A rare myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by sustained peripheral neutrophilia composed of mature segmented neutrophils and band forms
Splenomegaly and sometimes hepatomegaly are common, and the neutrophils lack significant dysplasia or a left shift to immature precursors
Activating mutations in the colony-stimulating factor 3 receptor gene (CSF3R), most often the T618I variant, are the characteristic molecular driver
Diagnosis requires exclusion of a reactive leukaemoid reaction and of other myeloproliferative neoplasms, particularly BCR-ABL1 positive chronic myeloid leukaemia
Unlike a reactive process, the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score tends to be normal or raised and there is no infective or inflammatory driver
Coexisting plasma cell disorders can drive a reactive neutrophilia that mimics the condition, so a monoclonal protein should be sought
CSF3R mutation status guides prognosis and targeted approaches such as JAK pathway inhibition
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm in which activating mutations of the granulocyte colony-stimulating factor receptor gene (CSF3R) drive unchecked signalling through the JAK/STAT and SRC-family kinase pathways. This produces sustained expansion of the mature neutrophil compartment without the dysplasia or maturation arrest seen in other myeloid disorders. The proliferating granulocytes accumulate in blood, marrow and spleen. Over time additional mutations may accrue and the disease can transform to acute leukaemia. A morphologically similar picture can be produced reactively by cytokines from an occult plasma cell neoplasm, which must be distinguished.
additionalDifferentials: Neutrophilia secondary to a plasma cell neoplasm
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film to characterise mature neutrophilia
BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis to exclude a plasma cell driver
Inflammatory and infective screen to exclude a reactive cause
redFlags: Rising blast count indicating transformation to acute leukaemia
Progressive anaemia or thrombocytopenia signalling marrow failure
reference.prognosis: The clinical course is variable; some patients remain stable for years while others progress to marrow failure or transform to acute myeloid leukaemia, and outcome is influenced by mutation burden and additional cytogenetic changes.
pitfalls: Accepting a reactive leukaemoid reaction as the diagnosis without molecular confirmation
Failing to exclude BCR-ABL1 positive chronic myeloid leukaemia
Missing an occult plasma cell neoplasm driving the neutrophilia
Overlooking CSF3R testing that establishes the diagnosis and informs therapy
management: Cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide to control mature neutrophilia and splenomegaly
JAK inhibition (ruxolitinib) guided by the activating CSF3R mutation, commonly the T618I variant
Exclusion and treatment of an underlying plasma cell neoplasm that can drive a mimicking reactive neutrophilia
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the sole curative option in suitable candidates
Supportive care addressing thrombotic risk and symptom control
Serial monitoring of blood counts, spleen size and blast burden with cytogenetic reassessment
Surveillance for transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia within haematology multidisciplinary care
